summaries.summary: Zipf's Law motivates character-composed distributed representations of social media posts to generalize to out-of-vocabulary words and unseen sequences at test time.
Traditional NNLMs use fixed word vocabularies and `UNKNOWN', while BIBREF2's bidirectional LSTM composes word vectors from characters.
The authors extend character modeling to unicode Twitter text, citing noisy slang, misspellings, emojis, 2 million tweets, and about 0.92 million unique word types.
Hashtags provide supervision for learning text representations, so the training objective predicts hashtags from latent representations using cross-entropy loss.
The proposed Bi-GRU tweet2vec combines final forward and backward GRU states into tweet embeddings and predicts hashtags through a softmax layer.
Neural distributed word representations from BIBREF0 and word2vec require large vector tables, struggle with unseen words, and need word-boundary preprocessing.
BIBREF2's bidirectional LSTM composes word embeddings from characters, whereas tweet2vec generates vector representations of entire tweets from characters.
This work adds to character models applied to Named Entity Recognition, POS tagging, text classification, and language modeling.
BIBREF14 estimated rare word representations from morphemes, but required a morpheme parser and faced a still-large morpheme space.
Earlier hashtag prediction work includes BIBREF15 and BIBREF16, with BIBREF15 using word lookup embeddings and showing generalization to document recommendation.
Figure 1 shows the Bi-GRU Encoder, which resembles the C2W model in BIBREF2 but replaces LSTM units with GRU units.
Characters from alphabet $C$ are one-hot encoded, projected by $P_C \in \mathbb {R}^{|C| \times d_c}$, and processed by forward-GRU and backward-GRU equations.
Reset and update gates, candidate output state, matrix dimensions, and final forward-GRU and backward GRU states are described for the GRU encoder.
Eq. 3 defines $e_t = W^f h_m^f + W^b h_0^b$.
$W^f, W^b$ are $d_t \times d_h$, $b$ is $d_t \times 1$, $d_t=d_h$ in experiments, and all parameters are learned using gradient descent.
The tweet embedding passes through a linear layer sized to the number of hashtags $L$, followed by a softmax layer.
Eq. 4 gives $P(y=j |e) = \frac{exp(w_j^Te + b_j)}{\sum _{i=1}^L exp(w_i^Te + b_j)}$.
The objective function optimizes categorical cross-entropy loss between predicted and true hashtags.
Eq. 5 defines $J = \frac{1}{B} \sum _{i=1}^{B} \sum _{j=1}^{L} -t_{i,j}log(p_{i,j}) + \lambda \Vert \Theta \Vert ^2$.
$B$ is batch size, $L$ is number of classes, $p_{i,j}$ is predicted probability, $t_{i,j} \in \lbrace 0,1\rbrace $ is ground truth, and L2-regularization is weighted by $\lambda $.
A word-level encoder splits tweets on white-spaces, uses the same architecture as tweet2vec, and stores vectors for the $V$ (20K here) most common words.
The Twitter dataset spans June 1, 2013 to June 5, 2013, filters hashtags $<500$ and $>19K$ posts, and contains 2 million training, 10K validation, 50K testing tweets, and 2039 distinct hashtags.
Word and character vectors use $d_L=150$, with 2829 unique characters, $B=64$, $\eta _0=0.01$, $\mu _0=0.9$, $\lambda =0.001$, $\sigma =0.1$, and convergence in about 20 epochs.
Hashtag prediction on a held-out test set reports average precision@1, recall@10, and mean rank of correct hashtags in Table 3.
Two test sets each containing 2,000 posts evaluate rare words (RW) and frequent words (FW), with tweet2vec significantly better on RW and comparably on FW.
Word model vocabulary sizes $V$ of 8K, 15K and 20K and tweet2vec GRU hidden state sizes 300, 400 and 500 show tweet2vec outperforming the word based model.
Table 4 compares models on small, medium and large datasets with increasing numbers of hashtags, and tweet2vec outperforms its word-based counterpart in all three settings.
Table 1 predictions highlight tweet2vec's robustness to word segmentation errors, spelling mistakes, emojis, special characters, and comparable performance on in-vocabulary tokens.
tweet2vec is a hashtag-supervised character level encoder that outperforms the word based approach, especially with many rare words, and may be extended to other languages and unseen hashtags.
The authors thank Alex Smola, Yun Fu, Hsiao-Yu Fish Tung, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Barnabas Poczos, Juergen Pfeffer, and reviewers.
